subtype: Approach: negotiating a shared decision with parents [Action]
passage: Ishan, you want to argue with your parents? Let me tell you how your cousin Aditi did it, and I am Ritu, her mother. When she was fifteen she came to us with one page. Three streams, the fees, the careers each one opens, and her own marks beside them. She said, "Can we look at this together?" Her father had already decided, and I had my worries. But nobody was telling anybody what to do; we were pointing at columns. Her father pointed at the fees. I pointed at her marks. By the end we had a compromise: Commerce with Maths, and a review after the first year. I still keep that page in a drawer.

qa.a: It compared three streams, their fees, the careers each one opens and her own marks.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she asked "Can we look at this together?"
qa.a: That her parents would weigh evidence with her instead of simply deciding, so she was hopeful and probably a little nervous.

qa.q: What could Aditi do if her parents disagree with one of her numbers?
qa.a: Ask which number they would change and why, and check the source together, because it keeps the talk about evidence.

qa.q: How did the conversation feel to Ritu?
qa.a: Less like a contest and more like solving a problem, since nobody was telling anybody what to do, and Ritu still keeps the page.

grounding: A student prepares a one-page comparison of fees, careers and her marks and asks her parents to review it together, and a compromise emerges.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a shared decision with parents [Action]
passage: Papa was leaving for a two-week posting on Monday, and the admission form had to be signed before then. Every talk so far had ended with "We know what's best." So on Saturday night Jahnavi printed one page. Three columns: Science with Maths, Commerce, Humanities with Psychology. Rows for fees, where each path could lead, and her own marks in each subject over two years. Her Maths had dropped every term; her Psychology project had got the top grade. She put the page on the dining table after dinner. "Can we look at this together? You can argue with the numbers." Her brother Ujjwal made a show of leaving the room. Papa read it twice. Mummy asked about Psychology careers. Nobody raised their voice. By eleven they had a compromise: Humanities with Psychology, plus Maths as an elective, and a review at the end of Class 11.

qa.q: Which three options were on Jahnavi's page?
qa.a: Science with Maths, Commerce, and Humanities with Psychology.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say they could argue with the numbers?
qa.a: She was probably nervous after earlier talks ended with "We know what's best", and hoped facts would feel less like defiance.

qa.q: What made the conversation work this time?
qa.a: One clear page with fees, careers and her marks let the family weigh evidence together instead of arguing about who decides.

qa.q: How might Papa see the compromise?
qa.a: Papa keeps Maths in the picture and a review point, so he may feel reassured that his concerns were heard before he leaves.

grounding: Shows a student bringing a one-page comparison to her parents under time pressure, shifting the talk to evidence and reaching a compromise.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a shared decision with parents [Action]
passage: Noor's parents had said no to Humanities three times at the dinner table in their Hyderabad flat, and each time Noor had cried and left. This time her cousin Lavanya, in second-year college, helped her do it differently. They made a single page: Commerce, Humanities with Fine Arts, and Science. Fees for each, the jobs people from her school had gone into, and Noor's marks over the last two years. Art: top of the class every term. Accounts: barely passing. On Sunday afternoon Noor laid the page in front of Ammi and Abbu. "I'm not asking you to agree. Just to read it with me." Abbu read slowly, pen in hand, and circled the fees for design college. Ammi asked what a graphic designer actually did all day. They talked for an hour. In the end: Humanities with Fine Arts, plus a Commerce elective, "for safety", Abbu said.

qa.q: What was Noor's record in Art?
qa.a: Top of the class every term.

qa.q: How had Noor been feeling after the earlier dinner-table talks?
qa.a: She felt upset and hurt, crying and leaving each time her parents said no.

qa.q: Why did the page help more than the earlier arguments?
qa.a: It moved the talk from who decides to weighing fees, careers and her marks together, so her parents could see the evidence.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel about the Commerce elective?
qa.a: Abbu seems reassured by it, calling it "for safety", so the compromise respects his worry while giving Noor her main choice.

grounding: Shows a student asking her parents to review a one-page comparison together, turning a standoff into weighing evidence and a compromise.
